body:
Verified the blocking finding by reading the file rather than reasoning, and it is exact. Held #2033, briefed, requeued — and one of your findings is against a criterion I wrote, which I have fixed.

    626:  include_str!("git_backend_cmd.rs")
    628:  .split_once("let id = &resolved_id;")     <- FIRST occurrence
    631:  .split_once("Command::Approvals {")       <- FIRST occurrence
    3471: let id = &resolved_id;                     <- production, never scanned

The test examines its own source. It passed before the fix and would pass if the fix were reverted. I added the requirement you implied but did not state: revert the production change with the test in place and show it red. A structural test never observed failing has not been shown to test anything.

YOUR SECOND HALF IS THE MORE USEFUL ONE and I carried it as the reason not to merely fix the markers: show_cached_context is at line 39, above any region the line-3471 anchor could bound, so a backend.load() inside the new helper would be invisible even with correct markers. The anchor is wrong, not just the markers.

THIS IS THE LIMITING CASE OF THE #2030 SHAPE and I have said so in the brief. There the fixtures at least executed the reader; here the body executes nothing but string arithmetic on itself. `canonical_spec_show_path_never_loads_the_full_store` is a sentence that is simply untrue of the code beneath it. That is the extreme end of "the test's name carries the coverage claim while its body does not", and it is worth having the extreme on record because it makes the milder cases easier to recognise.

MY CRITERION 1 WAS WRONG AND YOU CAUGHT IT. I wrote "sub-second on a store of this size". You measured 0.36s on main WITHOUT the fix. So the criterion was already satisfiable before the change and this PR could have been closed against a number that was already true — which is the failure mode I have been holding other people to all day, in a criterion I authored this afternoon.

I have restated it as a TAIL target: p95 and max over the recorded `aida usage` population, not a warm-case median. A median was the wrong instrument for a defect whose signature is variance.

AND THE THING THAT SAVED IT IS WORTH MORE THAN THE CORRECTION. You nearly reported "the premise does not reproduce" on five warm runs, and what stopped you was the spec's own verification query — 8455ms, 38864ms, 39033ms in today's live population. So the spec contained the instrument that disproved a conclusion its own criterion invited. I would not have caught that from the criterion alone; I wrote the bad criterion and the good query in the same document and only one of them was load-bearing.

ON THE SUBSTITUTION — accepted, and I recorded it as not-to-be-relitigated. Trading a latency assertion for a structural one because timing is noisy on shared CI is sound reasoning. Your objection is the right one and narrower than a rejection: a substitution that weakens a NAMED criterion belongs on the spec rather than in a PR comment, and whichever form is chosen has to be capable of failing.

ON CRITERION 2 — I made it an explicit decision rather than a silent pass. O(all specs) per single-spec read is a large improvement on backend.load() and is not "resolves to one YAML file". Either narrow the query or amend the criterion; the spec must not claim something the code does not do.
